How Distributed Teams Really Work

Distributed teams succeed when they replace office habits with deliberate ones: writing first, agreeing how and when to communicate, and building trust through visible work. This module gives you the operating model, a working agreement you can adopt with any team, and the leadership habits that keep people connected across distance.

Describe the kinds of distributed teams you are likely to join or lead

A distributed team is any team whose members do not share one workplace every day. It might be a company with staff in Lagos, Nairobi and London, a Nigerian NGO with coordinators in every state, a volunteer network spread across several African countries, or a freelancer working with a client abroad. What they all lose is the office: the quick question across the desk, the overheard update, the manager who can see who is busy. What they must build instead is a way of working that does not depend on everyone being online at the same moment.
Team members working from different locations connected online
A distributed team shares goals and documents, not a room.
Two modes of communication

**Synchronous** (sync) communication happens in real time: a phone call, a video meeting, a live chat where both people reply at once. **Asynchronous** (async) communication does not need an instant reply: a shared document, an email, a task comment, a well-written WhatsApp or Slack message that the reader can answer within agreed hours. Neither is better in every case. Sync is fast for feelings, conflict, brainstorming and emergencies. Async is better for updates, decisions that need thought, and anything that people in other time zones must read.

Many mature remote companies describe themselves as **async-first** (sometimes called async by default). GitLab, which publishes its whole remote handbook online, is a well known example. Async-first does not mean no meetings. It means a meeting is a deliberate choice, and the default is to write things down where everyone can find them. The benefit is that people can do focused work for long stretches, and a colleague eight hours away is not left out of decisions.

The escalation ladder
A simple rule keeps a team calm: start with the least interrupting channel that will still work in time, and move up only when you must. Each step up interrupts more people and costs more attention.
Phone call: emergencies only
Video call: conflict, complex talks
Direct message: needed today
Team channel: needed this week
Shared document or task comment
Begin at the wide base and climb only when urgency or emotion demands it.
Writing a message that does not need a meeting

The core skill of async work is writing a message complete enough that the reader can act without asking you anything. A useful check is the **five parts**: context (what this is about), the ask (exactly what you need), the deadline (when, with the time zone), the options or your recommendation, and where the supporting material lives. Put the ask in the first line, because many people read only the preview on their phone.
Worked example: turning a vague ping into a complete async message

For example, Amaka coordinates a training programme. Her colleague Tunde in Abuja and the funder's officer in London must approve a venue. Her first draft in the team chat was: "Hi, are you free? Need to talk about the venue."
She notices the draft has no ask, no deadline and forces a live conversation.
First line: "Decision needed by Thursday 5 pm Lagos time (WAT): approve Venue B for the March workshop."
Context: two venues were quoted; Venue A is about 450,000 naira for two days, Venue B about 380,000 naira (approximate quotes, valid for 7 days).
Recommendation: Venue B, because it has a backup generator and is 10 minutes from the bus park; the difference is 70,000 naira (450,000 minus 380,000).
Where to look: both quotes and photos are in the shared folder "March Workshop / Venues", with the link pasted.
Fallback: "If I hear nothing by the deadline I will book Venue B so we keep the date."
Tunde approves with a thumbs-up and one comment; the funder replies the next morning in her own working hours. No meeting was needed and the decision is on record.
Silence is not agreement unless you say so
A stated fallback ("if no objection by Thursday, I will proceed") turns silence into a clear rule. Use it only for decisions you are allowed to make, and always say what you will do.
Where these skills are used
**Fully remote companies** where everyone works from home or co-working spaces and there is no head office.
**Hybrid teams** where some people share an office and others dial in; the remote people are easily forgotten unless the team writes things down.
**Multi-site organisations** such as NGOs, banks or churches with offices in several cities or countries.
**Contractor and freelance networks** where a client brings together people from different firms and countries for a project.
**Volunteer networks** where people give a few hours a week, often by phone, and cannot attend long calls.

In every one of these, people who lead, coordinate or support the team are judged less on how many hours they are online and more on whether others can see progress, find decisions and rely on what was promised. That is what the rest of this course builds.

The team working agreement: channels, response times and overlap hours
List the sections of a team working agreement

Most remote frustration comes from unspoken expectations. One person thinks a WhatsApp message deserves a reply within ten minutes; another checks messages twice a day. One person keeps files on their laptop; another expects them in the shared drive. A **team working agreement** (also called a team charter or communication charter) writes these expectations down so they can be discussed, agreed and changed. It is short, usually one or two pages, and every new member reads it in their first week.

Working out overlap hours

Overlap hours are the times when everyone is inside their normal working day. To find them, convert every person's hours into one reference time, usually **UTC** (Coordinated Universal Time), then find where the ranges meet. Nigeria uses West Africa Time (WAT), which is UTC+1 all year with no daylight saving. Kenya uses East Africa Time, UTC+3, also with no daylight saving. The United Kingdom is UTC+0 in winter and UTC+1 in summer (British Summer Time), and Toronto is UTC-5 in winter and UTC-4 in summer. Because some countries change their clocks, **overlap can shift twice a year**, so check it in March and in October or November.
Worked example: a four-city team in January
For example, Ifeoma leads a project team in January. Members work 9 am to 5 pm local time in Lagos (UTC+1), Nairobi (UTC+3), London (UTC+0) and Toronto (UTC-5).
Lagos 9 to 17 local is 08:00 to 16:00 UTC (subtract 1 hour).
Nairobi 9 to 17 local is 06:00 to 14:00 UTC (subtract 3 hours).
London 9 to 17 local is 09:00 to 17:00 UTC (no change in winter).
Toronto 9 to 17 local is 14:00 to 22:00 UTC (add 5 hours).
All four together: the latest start is 14:00 UTC (Toronto) and the earliest finish is 14:00 UTC (Nairobi), so there is no shared hour at all.
Without Toronto: 09:00 to 14:00 UTC, which is 10 am to 3 pm in Lagos, 5 hours of overlap.
Toronto with Lagos and London: 14:00 to 16:00 UTC, which is 3 pm to 5 pm in Lagos and 9 am to 11 am in Toronto.

Ifeoma does not force a four-city meeting. She sets a weekly 3 pm WAT call for Lagos, London and Toronto, a 10 am WAT check-in that includes Nairobi, and makes the written weekly update the place where all four meet.

Response times that people can keep

Response-time rules must be realistic for the slowest normal situation, not the best day. A coordinator in a rural area with unstable power and costly data cannot promise a ten-minute reply. A good agreement separates channels by urgency and gives one clear route for emergencies, so that nobody feels they must watch every chat all evening. It also protects rest: if the agreement says messages after 6 pm local time can wait until the next working day, people can switch off their notifications without guilt.

Trust at a distance: visibility, accountability and psychological safety
Explain why remote trust rests on visible, reliable work rather than presence
Run a useful one-to-one meeting with a remote team member
Handle disagreement in text before it becomes conflict
Apply practices that make quieter and low-bandwidth members heard

In an office, a manager often judges commitment by who arrives early and who looks busy. Remote teams cannot do that, and they should not try. Trust on a distributed team is built on three visible things: **people do what they said, by when they said, and say early when they cannot**. Leaders who try to replace presence with surveillance, such as demanding cameras on all day or counting online minutes, usually damage trust and get worse work.
Team members celebrating together
Trust grows when people can see progress and feel safe to speak.
Manage outcomes, not hours

Agree what a good result looks like, the deadline and who owns it, then let people organise their own time. This matters especially where members juggle family duties, power cuts and commuting to a place with stable internet. A useful habit is the **commitment message**: when you accept a task, you reply with what you will deliver and by when. When something slips, you post an update before the deadline, not after it.
The remote trust cycle
Make a clear commitment
Deliver or flag early
Work is visible to others
Others rely on you more
Each kept or honestly renegotiated promise makes the next one easier to believe.
Psychological safety

Psychological safety, a term developed by Harvard Business School professor Amy Edmondson, means people believe they will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns or mistakes. Remote teams need it more, not less, because problems hidden at a distance grow quietly. You build it by thanking people who raise bad news early, by admitting your own mistakes in the team channel, and by asking direct questions such as "What could go wrong with this plan?" rather than "Any questions?".
The remote one-to-one

A regular one-to-one (1:1) is the leader's most important meeting. Keep a shared running document for each person, so both of you add topics during the week and nothing is lost. A practical rhythm is 30 minutes every one or two weeks, by voice call if data is costly.
**Their agenda first:** what is on your mind, what is blocking you?
**Progress against commitments**, using the task board rather than memory.
**Feedback both ways:** one thing to keep doing, one thing to change, and ask what you as leader should change.
**Growth:** a skill they want to build this quarter.
**Actions written in the shared document** before you hang up.
Disagreement in text

Written messages lose tone, and short replies can read as cold. Two rules prevent most remote conflict. First, **assume good intent and ask before reacting**: "When you wrote 'this won't work', do you mean the timeline or the budget?" Second, **move to voice after two rounds**: if a disagreement has gone back and forth twice in a chat, call, settle it, then post a written summary so others see the outcome.
Worked example: a tense thread

For example, Zainab, a programme officer in Kano, posts a draft report. Femi, the finance lead in Lagos, replies in the team channel: "These numbers are wrong again." Zainab feels embarrassed in front of twelve people.
Chiamaka, the team lead, sees the thread and messages Femi directly: "Can you list the specific lines so Zainab can fix them?"
Femi lists two lines: transport was entered as 85,000 naira but receipts total 58,000 naira, a transposed figure; and one per diem was counted twice.
Chiamaka calls Zainab for five minutes, shares the two lines, and asks what would help; Zainab suggests a shared checklist before reports are posted.
Zainab corrects the report. The transport line drops by 27,000 naira (85,000 minus 58,000).
Chiamaka posts in the channel: "Report corrected, thanks Zainab and Femi. From next month we will use a two-line finance check before posting drafts."
In the next working agreement review, the team adds: "Give critical feedback with specific lines, in a comment on the document rather than in the main channel."
The error is fixed, Zainab is not shamed, and the team gains a process that prevents the same problem.
Including everyone
Rotate meeting times when overlap is unfair, so the same people do not always join at night.
Send agendas early and accept written input from people who cannot join.
In calls, invite quieter people by name and use the chat for written contributions.
Offer audio-only or voice-note options for members on limited data.
Create small informal spaces, such as a weekly 15-minute optional chat or a channel for wins and photos, because remote teams lose casual connection.
Monitoring tools and privacy

Screenshot or keystroke tracking software collects personal data. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 governs how personal data is collected and used. Do not install monitoring on anyone's device without a lawful basis, clear written notice and advice from your organisation's data protection lead.
Remote trust comes from clear commitments, early flags and visible work, not from hours online.

A distributed team lives inside its tools. If files sit in personal laptops, decisions are buried in private chats and tasks live in people's heads, the team spends hours searching and asking. The fix is a **single source of truth**: for each kind of information, the team agrees one place where the current, correct version lives. Everything else, including chat messages, only points to that place.

Folders and file names

A shared drive becomes useless when every person invents their own structure. Agree a top level by area or project, a small fixed set of subfolders, and a naming pattern. A good pattern puts the date first in **YYYY-MM-DD** form, the international ISO 8601 format, so files sort in date order on any device.
Worked example: tidying an NGO programme drive

For example, Halima runs operations for a women's livelihood programme with coordinators in Kaduna, Enugu and Oyo. The drive has files named "final report.docx", "final report 2.docx" and "FINAL final (Ngozi).docx".
She creates one top-level folder per year, then one per project: "2026 / Livelihood Programme".
Inside each project she fixes five subfolders: 01 Admin, 02 Plans, 03 Field Data, 04 Reports, 05 Media.
She sets the naming pattern: date, project code, document type, version. Example: "2026-03-31_LIV_Q1-Report_v03".
She stops versions in file names for Google Docs, because Docs keep version history automatically; versions in names are kept only for PDFs sent outside.
She moves 214 old files in two afternoons and adds a one-page "How our drive works" note to the handbook.
She asks coordinators to share links, not attachments, in WhatsApp.
Coordinators find the current report in seconds, and nobody edits an out-of-date copy because there is only one.
Access and security
Turn on **two-step verification** for every work account, including WhatsApp, email and the drive.
Share folders with named people or the organisation, not "anyone with the link", when files contain personal data.
Give the least access needed: viewers who only read, editors who must change files.
Keep an access list. When someone leaves, remove their access the same day and transfer ownership of their files.
Store beneficiary or staff personal data only where the organisation has agreed, and collect only what is needed, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.
Phishing targets shared drives

Fake "document shared with you" emails are a common way to steal passwords. Before signing in, check the sender address and the web address. If unsure, open the drive directly from your own bookmark, not from the email link.
Start a small handbook

The knowledge base does not need to be large on day one. Start with one shared document called "How we work" and add a page each time someone asks the same question twice. Within a few months new members can answer most of their own questions, and the leader stops being the only place where knowledge lives.

Designing for low bandwidth

Some members will work on a phone with costly data or uncertain power. Make offline access possible (Google Docs and Sheets can be made available offline on phones), keep documents text-first with compressed images, and post a short text summary with every large file so people know whether to download it. Voice notes are useful for field updates, but ask for a two-line written summary with them so the information can be searched later.

From brief to delivery: owners, status updates and written decisions
Write a project brief that a remote colleague can start from without a meeting
Assign a single owner and use the DACI roles for decisions
Write a weekly async status update in a standard format
Hand over work across time zones without losing context

Remote work goes wrong in the gaps: unclear requests, two people each thinking the other owns a task, and decisions made on a call that half the team never hears about. A simple written workflow closes these gaps. It has four parts: a **brief** at the start, a single **owner** for each piece of work, a regular **status update**, and a **decision record** when choices are made.
A person checking items on a task list
Clear owners and written status keep remote work moving.
Remote delivery workflow
Written brief
Owner and deadline
Weekly status update
Decisions logged
Delivery and review
Every stage leaves a written trace that someone in another time zone can pick up.
The one-page brief
**Goal:** what success looks like, in one or two sentences.
**Deliverable:** exactly what will be handed over, in what format.
**Audience or user:** who it is for.
**Deadline and milestones**, with time zone.
**Constraints:** budget, brand rules, data rules, tools.
**Owner and reviewers:** who does it, who checks it, who approves.
**Links:** previous examples, data, templates.
One owner, clear decision roles

Every task needs one named owner, sometimes called the **DRI** (directly responsible individual). Others can help, but one person is accountable for moving it forward. For decisions, the **DACI** framework from Atlassian's Team Playbook gives four roles: the **Driver** gathers information and gets the decision made by the agreed date; the **Approver** is the one person who decides; **Contributors** give expert input, a voice but not a vote; and the **Informed** are told once it is decided. Naming these roles in writing ends the common remote problem of decisions that are discussed for weeks and never made.
The weekly async status update
Replace most status meetings with a written update posted on a fixed day, in the same format every time, so readers know where to look. A widely used structure is:
**Status line:** On track, At risk or Off track, with one sentence why.
**Done this week:** finished items with links.
**Next week:** planned items with owners and dates.
**Blocked or at risk:** what is stuck, who can unblock it, by when.
**Decisions needed:** the question, options, recommendation and Approver.
Worked example: a status update and a DACI decision
For example, Kemi owns a community health awareness campaign run by a team in Lagos, Port Harcourt and Accra. It is Friday and she posts her update in the campaign channel and the project document.
Status: At risk. Radio slots are booked but the flyer artwork is 3 days late.
Done: 4 of 6 radio jingles recorded (links); volunteer list confirmed at 38 people.
Next: Seun in Port Harcourt records the last 2 jingles by Wednesday; Kwame in Accra finalises the flyer by Tuesday 5 pm WAT (4 pm in Accra, which is UTC+0).

Blocked: printing takes 5 working days; if Kwame delivers on Tuesday, flyers are ready the following Tuesday (Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Monday, Tuesday), which is distribution day itself, with no buffer.

Decision needed, using DACI: print 5,000 flyers at about 45 naira each (about 225,000 naira) or 3,000 at about 55 naira each (about 165,000 naira); quotes approximate. Driver: Kemi. Approver: the programme manager, Bola. Contributors: finance and Seun. Informed: all volunteers.
Kemi recommends 3,000 flyers, because 38 volunteers can realistically hand out about 80 each, which is 3,040 flyers.
Bola approves the 3,000 option in a comment on Saturday. Kemi logs the decision with date, Approver and reason, and the volunteers are told on Monday.
Handovers across time zones

When work passes from one person to another at the end of their day, sometimes called a follow-the-sun handover, the receiver must be able to continue without asking anything. A good handover note says what was done, the exact state now, what to do next, known risks and where the files are. Write it in the task or document, not only in chat.
Red early is better than green late
Mark work At risk the moment you doubt the date. Leaders can usually fix a problem with three days' notice; they rarely can with three hours.
A handover note that works
**Done:** "Cleaned the March attendance sheet; 214 rows, duplicates removed."
**State now:** "Draft chart is in the Q1 Report document, section 3, not yet checked."
**Next action:** "Check the Oyo totals against the field forms in 03 Field Data, then share with Bola."
**Risks:** "Two Oyo forms were unreadable photos; I asked the coordinator to resend."
**Where:** links to every file mentioned.

Common brief mistakes are just as predictable: no deadline time zone, two people named as owner, no link to previous examples, and a goal written as an activity ("run a campaign") instead of a result ("3,000 flyers reach women in four markets by 30 April"). Read your brief once as if you were new to the team, and fix anything you would need to ask about.
Start work from a one-page written brief.
Give every task one owner and every decision a Driver and a single Approver (DACI).

Ask a colleague to read both without explanation and note any question they still have.

Meetings that earn their time: agendas, roles and written summaries
Decide whether a topic needs a meeting at all
Write an agenda that states the outcome needed for each item
Run a remote meeting with clear roles and inclusive habits
Produce a written summary and decision log entry within one working day

Remote meetings are expensive. A one-hour call with eight people uses eight hours of the team's time, plus the focus lost before and after, plus data costs for people on mobile connections. In an async-first team a meeting has to earn its place. Before you book one, ask: could this be a document with comments? If the honest answer is yes, write the document.
People joining a video meeting from different screens
A good remote meeting starts before the call and ends with a written record.
When a meeting is the right tool
Meet or write?
Meet live
Write async
Sensitive feedback or conflict
Brainstorming many ideas fast
Urgent incident response
Building relationships, new team members
Status updates
Information sharing
Decisions needing data and reading
Review of a draft
If a topic sits on the right, a document with comments is usually faster and fairer.
An agenda that drives outcomes

Post the agenda at least 24 hours before, in the shared meeting document, with pre-reads linked. Write each item as a question with the outcome you need: decide, agree, gather input or inform. Put a time against each item and the name of the person leading it. If there is no agenda, it is reasonable for people to ask for one or to decline.

**Facilitator:** keeps to the agenda, invites quieter people by name, parks off-topic issues.
**Note-taker:** writes decisions and actions live in the shared document so everyone can see them.
**Timekeeper:** warns at the halfway and two-minute points of each item.
**Decision owner:** for each decision item, the Approver who confirms the choice aloud.

Rotate these roles so the same person, often the most junior woman in the room, is not always the note-taker. Start on time, and do not repeat the meeting for late joiners; the live notes will catch them up. If you record the call, tell everyone at the start and explain where the recording will be kept and for how long, because recordings contain personal data.
The written summary

The meeting is not finished until the summary is posted, ideally the same day and certainly within one working day. People who could not attend should be able to act on it. Keep it short: decisions, actions with owners and dates, open questions, and a link to the full notes. Then copy each decision into the team's **decision log**, a simple table with date, decision, Approver, reason and link.
Worked example: costing and summarising a weekly call
For example, Ruth leads a seven-person regional team that met for 60 minutes every Monday. She wants to know what the meeting costs and whether it can be shorter.
Time cost: 7 people x 1 hour = 7 person-hours a week; over 4 weeks that is 28 person-hours.
She moves status updates to a written Friday post, which removes 25 minutes of reading out updates.
The new call is 30 minutes for decisions and risks only: 7 x 0.5 = 3.5 person-hours a week, 14 a month, saving 14 person-hours a month.

After the next call she posts: Decisions: Kaduna and Ekiti pilot the new form (Approver: Ruth). Actions: Ada sends the form to both coordinators by Wednesday; Musa lists June training risks in the risk sheet by Thursday. Open: venue for Ekiti, Musa to propose by next Monday.
She adds the pilot decision to the decision log with the reason: both states already use smartphones for reporting.
The team halves its meeting time, and people who missed the call act on the summary the same afternoon.
The two-minute read-back
End every meeting by having the note-taker read the actions aloud with owners and dates. It catches misunderstandings while everyone is still on the call.
Inclusive and hybrid calls
Share the agenda and pre-reads early so people with slower connections can download them in advance.
Allow cameras off when data or power is limited; ask for audio and chat contributions instead.
Use the chat or a shared document for round-robin input, so quieter people can write rather than interrupt.
In hybrid meetings, give remote people the first turn on each item, and have one person in the room watch the chat.
Keep calls under an hour; for longer work sessions, schedule a 10-minute break.

Hybrid meetings, where some people sit together in a room and others join online, are the hardest to run fairly. The people in the room talk to each other, side conversations are lost, and remote members struggle to break in. A simple rule many remote teams use is "one person, one screen": if anyone is remote, everyone joins from their own device, even people in the same office, so all voices sound and look equal. When that is not possible, use one good room microphone and a facilitator who reads the chat aloud.
Count meeting cost in person-hours, and turn status meetings into written updates.
Agenda items are questions with a stated outcome, posted 24 hours ahead with pre-reads.
Use and rotate roles: facilitator, note-taker, timekeeper, decision owner.
Post a summary within one working day and log every decision.

Diagnosing, Improving and Leading Distributed Teams

In this final module you learn to assess how well a distributed team is working, scope and price an improvement plan as a consultant or internal lead, and build the personal accountability system and evidence portfolio that show you can be trusted with remote leadership.
Diagnosing a distributed team: discovery questions and a collaboration audit
Ask discovery questions that reveal how a remote team really works
Score a team on eight collaboration areas using evidence
Prioritise fixes using an impact and effort matrix
Write a short findings summary for a team leader

Whether you are joining a new remote team, taking over as its lead, or being invited to advise an organisation, your first job is to understand how work actually flows today. Teams often describe the way they wish they worked. Your job is to find the way they really work, using questions and evidence, before you suggest anything.
Two people in a discovery conversation
Good diagnosis starts with listening and asking for evidence.
Discovery questions
Area
Question to ask
Evidence to request
When you need a quick answer, where do you ask, and how long do you usually wait?

Talk to people at different levels and locations, not only the leader, and speak to at least one person who joined recently. New joiners notice gaps that long-serving staff no longer see. Keep what people tell you confidential and report patterns, not names.
Scoring the audit

Score each of the eight areas from 1 to 5 using the evidence: 1 means no shared practice, 3 means a practice exists but is used unevenly, 5 means a written practice that most people follow. Scores are a tool for conversation, not a verdict, so show the evidence behind each number.
Worked example: auditing a volunteer network

For example, Grace is asked to review a women's volunteer network with coordinators in six Nigerian states and two in Ghana. She interviews nine people and reviews two weeks of messages and documents.
Scores: Channels 2, Source of truth 1, Ownership 3, Updates 2, Meetings 3, Decisions 1, Onboarding 2, Wellbeing and inclusion 3.
Total is 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 17 out of a possible 40; the average is 17 / 8 = 2.1.
Evidence for Source of truth: it took 11 minutes and three people to find the current volunteer list, and two versions disagreed by 23 names.
Evidence for Decisions: a change to the reporting date was agreed on a call but never written down; three coordinators missed it.
Evidence for Wellbeing: 40% of the group messages she reviewed (62 of 155) were sent after 9 pm, often by the same two coordinators.
Grace reports that the two lowest areas, Source of truth and Decisions, are causing visible errors, and recommends starting there.
Choosing what to fix first

Do not try to fix everything. Place each possible improvement on an **impact and effort matrix**: how much it would help, against how hard it is to do. Start with high-impact, low-effort quick wins, plan the high-impact, high-effort projects, and drop most low-impact work.
Impact and effort matrix
Quick wins: do now
Big projects: plan carefully
Small tidy-ups: if time
Avoid: low value, costly
Effort (low to high)
Impact (high to low)
A decision log is a quick win; moving the whole organisation to a new tool is a big project.

For Grace's network, a shared decision log and one master volunteer list are quick wins: a few hours each, with immediate effect. A full handbook is a big project for the following quarter. Buying a paid project tool is in the avoid box for now, because the problem is habit, not software.
The findings summary
One-sentence overall picture, for example "Strong commitment, weak shared records."
The scores table with one line of evidence per area.
Top three recommendations, each with owner, effort and expected effect.
What you did not look at, so the leader knows the limits of the review.
A proposed date to re-score in 60 to 90 days.
Handle message reviews carefully

Reading a team's chats can expose personal information. Get written permission from the organisation, tell members a review is happening, look only at work channels, and never copy private details into your report.
When you are the new member

The same questions help when you join a remote team rather than advise one. In your first week ask your manager or a buddy: Which channel do I use for what? How quickly do people expect replies? Where are decisions recorded? Which meetings must I attend and which are optional? What does a good weekly update look like here? Write the answers down. If no working agreement exists, your notes can become the first draft of one, which is a useful early contribution.
Ask for evidence, not just opinions: "show me where the current version is".
Interview across levels and locations, including a recent joiner.
Score eight areas from 1 to 5 and show the evidence for each score.
Start with high-impact, low-effort fixes and state the limits of your review.

Scoping, pricing and protecting a collaboration improvement project
Turn audit findings into a scoped improvement project with deliverables
Estimate effort in days and calculate a fair project price
Write a short proposal with acceptance criteria and payment terms
Handle extra requests with a written change request

After an audit, the leader usually asks: "Can you help us fix this?" You might answer as an external consultant who charges a fee, or as an internal lead who must win time and support from management. Either way, the same discipline applies: define exactly what will be delivered, estimate the effort honestly, agree how success will be judged, and protect the scope from quietly growing.
A signed project document
A short written scope protects both you and the client.
From findings to deliverables

Turn each recommendation into something that can be handed over and checked. "Improve communication" is not a deliverable. "A one-page working agreement, agreed by all coordinators and published in the handbook" is. Good deliverables for this kind of project include a working agreement, a tidied shared drive with naming rules, a decision log template, a status update template, a meeting format, a short handbook, and training sessions with recordings or notes.
From audit to agreed project
Audit findings
Deliverables and acceptance criteria
Effort estimate in days
Price and payment terms
Signed scope
Every price should trace back to named deliverables and estimated days.
Estimating and pricing

A simple, defensible method is a **day rate** multiplied by estimated days. Work out your day rate from the income you need and the days you can realistically bill. Remember that as an independent consultant you will not bill every working day: some days go to finding clients, admin, learning and rest. Add a small contingency for unknowns, and say clearly what is not included.
Worked example: pricing a 10-day engagement

For example, Bimpe is an independent remote-operations consultant in Ibadan. An Abuja-based NGO with 15 staff across four states asks her to fix the problems found in her audit. The figures below are illustrative, not market rates.
Day rate: she aims for 800,000 naira a month before costs and expects to bill about 10 days a month, so 800,000 / 10 = 80,000 naira per day.

Effort: audit already done; working agreement workshop and drafting 2 days; drive restructure and naming rules 3 days; templates for status updates, meetings and decision log 2 days; two 2-hour training sessions with preparation 2 days; 30-day follow-up review 1 day. Total: 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10 days.
Base price: 10 x 80,000 = 800,000 naira.
Contingency of 10% for unknowns: 800,000 x 0.10 = 80,000 naira, giving a fixed price of 880,000 naira.
Payment terms: 50% on signing (440,000 naira) and 50% on acceptance of the deliverables (440,000 naira), paid by bank transfer to her business account.
Out of scope, written in the proposal: buying or configuring paid software, migrating email systems, and work for teams outside the four states.
The NGO accepts a clear, traceable price. Both sides know exactly what 880,000 naira buys.
Acceptance criteria

For each deliverable, agree how it will be judged finished. For example: "Working agreement: signed off by the programme manager and posted in the handbook"; "Drive: all current-year files moved into the new structure and three coordinators can find the current budget in under one minute". Acceptance criteria stop the endless "just one more change" at the end of a project.
Protecting the scope

Scope creep is when extra work slips in without extra time or money. In remote projects it often arrives as a casual WhatsApp message: "While you are at it, can you also set up the board for the finance team?" Do not refuse and do not silently agree. Reply that you are happy to help and will send a short change request.
Describe the new request in one or two sentences.
Estimate extra days and cost: for example, 2 extra days x 80,000 = 160,000 naira.
State the effect on the timeline, for example the final review moves by one week.
Ask the approver named in the contract to accept in writing (an email reply is enough).
Start the extra work only after written approval, and log it with the project decisions.
Payments and fraud

Confirm bank details by phone with a known contact before any transfer, and be suspicious of sudden "new account" instructions by email or WhatsApp, a common fraud pattern. If you are registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) as a business name or company, invoice in that name so payments go to your business account.
If you are an internal lead
Use the same structure in an internal proposal, replacing the price with the hours you and others will need, and the payment terms with the approval you need from management.
The one-page proposal

Keep the proposal short enough to read on a phone: the problem in two sentences using audit evidence; the deliverables with acceptance criteria; the timeline by week; the price, contingency and payment terms; what is out of scope; how changes will be handled; and the names of the client Approver and your own contact details. Send it as a PDF and ask for written acceptance by email, which becomes your record.
Turn findings into named deliverables, each with acceptance criteria.
Price = day rate x estimated days, plus a stated contingency; list what is out of scope.
Agree payment terms such as 50% on signing and 50% on acceptance.
Handle extra requests with a written change request before starting the work.

Take the top three recommendations from your mini audit.
Turn each into a deliverable with an acceptance criterion.
Estimate days for each, calculate a price from a day rate you can justify (or hours for an internal proposal), and add contingency.
List at least three items that are out of scope.

Your accountability system, leadership portfolio and 90-day plan
Set up a personal system to capture, plan and review your commitments
Use start-of-day and end-of-day posts to keep your work visible
Measure your own reliability with a simple commitment tracker
Assemble a three-piece evidence portfolio and a 90-day plan

Leaders of distributed teams are trusted when their own work is reliable and visible. Nobody walks past your desk to see that you are busy, so you need a personal system that keeps track of every promise and makes progress easy for others to see. This lesson helps you build that system and then package your evidence for employers, clients or your own organisation.
A person concentrating on focused work at a desk
A personal system frees your mind for focused work.
Capture, plan, do, review

David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD) method is a widely used personal productivity approach. Its core idea is that your mind is for having ideas, not holding them: capture every commitment into one trusted list, decide the next action, organise it, and review the system weekly. You can run it in a notebook, Google Tasks, Microsoft To Do or a simple sheet.
Weekly accountability cycle
Capture every commitment
Plan the week Monday
Time-block focus work
Post visible updates
Review on Friday
The Friday review feeds the next Monday plan, so nothing promised is forgotten.
**Capture:** every time you say "I will" in a message or call, add it to your list within the hour, with a date.
**Plan Monday:** choose the three most important outcomes for the week and block time for them in your calendar, inside your best working hours.
**Protect focus:** set your status to Focus during those blocks and mute non-urgent channels, as your working agreement allows.

**Make it visible:** post a short start-of-day line ("Today: finish the Q1 report draft, review Musa's budget") and an end-of-day line ("Done: draft shared. Tomorrow: budget review. Blocked: none") in the team channel if your team uses them.
**Review Friday:** check every commitment, close finished ones, renegotiate any that will slip before their date, and write next week's top three.
Measure your reliability

Keep a simple commitment tracker: date promised, what, due date, outcome (on time, renegotiated early, late). Review it monthly. The goal is not perfection but honesty: a commitment changed early with a reason is far better for trust than one missed silently.
Worked example: four weeks of commitments
For example, Uche coordinates a remote training team and tracks every commitment she makes for four weeks.
She records 14 commitments in total.
12 were delivered on time, 1 was renegotiated two days before its due date, and 1 was delivered late without warning.
On-time rate: 12 / 14 = 0.857, about 86%.
Kept or renegotiated early: 13 / 14 = 0.929, about 93%.
She looks at the late item: it was promised in a voice call and never captured in her list.
Her fix: after every call she spends two minutes moving any "I will" into her list before doing anything else.
The next month Uche records 15 commitments with none late without warning, and her team lead notices she is easy to rely on.
Your evidence portfolio

Remote employers and clients increasingly ask for proof of how you work, not just a CV. Build a short portfolio, as a shared folder or a page on a free site such as Google Sites, containing three pieces. Remove names and personal or confidential details from real documents, or use practice versions.
Piece
What it shows
Include
Async status update
You write clearly for readers in other places and times
One weekly update with status, done, next, blocked, decisions needed
Meeting pack
You run meetings that produce decisions
Agenda, posted summary and decision log entry for the same meeting
Accountability system
You keep promises and make work visible
Screenshot of your list, one weekly review note, your commitment tracker summary
Add a half-page reflection: what you changed, what improved and what you would do differently. Concrete, honest reflection is more convincing than claims like "excellent communicator".
Boundaries protect reliability

Remote work can quietly stretch into every evening, especially when colleagues are in other time zones. A reliable leader is a rested one. Set clear end-of-day times in your calendar and status, turn off notifications for non-urgent channels outside working hours, and use scheduled sending so your late-night messages arrive in the morning. If you lead others, model this yourself: when the leader replies at midnight, the team believes midnight replies are expected.
Your 90-day plan
**Days 1 to 30:** run your accountability cycle every week; publish or update a working agreement with one team.
**Days 31 to 60:** run a mini audit on a team you belong to and deliver two quick wins, such as a decision log and a status update template.

**Days 61 to 90:** re-score the team, write a one-page before-and-after case study, and add it to your portfolio; apply for at least one remote coordination or team lead role, or offer the improvement project to one organisation.

Module 1 video
How distributed teams really work: write first, agree, build trust
How distributed teams really work.
This is the video for module one of Remote Work and Team Collaboration.
Why this matters
What a distributed team loses
No quick question across the desk
No overheard updates
Nobody can see who is busy
So we build deliberate habits instead
A distributed team is any team whose members do not share one workplace every day.
They lose the office: the quick question, the overheard update, the manager who can see who is busy.
So we build deliberate habits instead. Writing first, agreeing how we communicate, and building trust through visible work.
Two modes
Sync or async?
Sync: real time
Feelings and conflict
Brainstorming new ideas
Emergencies, like a site down
Async: reply later
Weekly progress updates
Decisions that need thought
Anything across time zones
Synchronous, or sync, means real time, like a phone or video call. It is fast for feelings, conflict, brainstorming and emergencies, because tone is easily misread in text.
Asynchronous, or async, means the reader can answer later, within agreed hours. It is better for updates, decisions that need thought, and other time zones.
Async-first does not mean no meetings. It means a meeting is a deliberate choice, and the default is to write things down.
Stay calm
Start with the least interrupting channel that will still work in time. The base is a shared document or task comment.
Then the team channel for this week, and a direct message for today.
Video calls are for conflict and complex talks. Phone calls are for emergencies only.
Each step up interrupts more people, so climb only as far as you must.
Core skill
A message that does not need a meeting
The ask: exactly what you need
Deadline, with the time zone
Context: what this is about
Options or your recommendation
Where the material lives
Put the ask in the first line. Many read only the preview.
The core skill of async work is a message so complete that the reader can act without asking you anything.
Use the five parts. The ask, exactly what you need, and the deadline with the time zone.
Then the context, and the options or your recommendation.
Finally, say where the supporting material lives, and paste the link.
Put the ask in the first line, because many people read only the preview on their phone.
Worked example
Amaka's venue decision
For example, Amaka needs Tunde in Abuja and a funder in London to approve a workshop venue.
Venue A, two days
Venue B, two days
Naira prices are approximate quotes.
Amaka's first draft said: Hi, are you free? Need to talk about the venue. It has no ask and no deadline.
Her rewrite starts: decision needed by Thursday 5 pm Lagos time, approve Venue B.
Venue A is about 450,000 naira for two days. Venue B is about 380,000 naira. These quotes are approximate.
She recommends Venue B, because it has a backup generator and is 10 minutes from the bus park.
She links the quotes and adds a fallback: if I hear nothing by the deadline, I will book Venue B. No meeting was needed.
Working agreement
Find your team's overlap hours
Collect everyone's working hours
Convert each one to UTC
Find where the ranges meet
Recheck when clocks change
Nigeria is UTC+1 all year, with no daylight saving.
A team working agreement writes down channels, reply times, working hours and where files live. One key part is overlap hours, when everyone is inside their working day.
Convert every person's hours into UTC, which means Coordinated Universal Time. For example, 9 to 5 in Lagos is 08:00 to 16:00 UTC.
When Ifeoma did this for Lagos, Nairobi, London and Toronto in January, there was no shared hour at all. So she held smaller calls, and the written weekly update became the place where all four meet.
Some countries change their clocks, so check overlap in March, and in October or November. Nigeria stays on UTC plus 1 all year.
Trust at a distance
Trust rests on three visible things
When you accept a task, reply with what you will deliver. Then deliver it.
Agree the result, the deadline and the owner. Manage outcomes, not hours online.
When something slips, post an update before the deadline, not after it.
Remote trust rests on three visible things. First, people do what they said. Reply to a task with what you will deliver.
Second, by when they said. Agree the result, deadline and owner, then let people organise their own time.
Third, say early when you cannot, before the deadline, not after.
The common mistake is surveillance, like demanding cameras on all day. That usually damages trust and gets worse work.
Key points
Remember
Sync for emotion and emergencies; async for the rest
Climb the escalation ladder only as far as needed
Ask, deadline with time zone, context, link
Convert hours to UTC to find overlap
Trust: commit, deliver or flag early, stay visible
To remember. Sync for emotion and emergencies, async for updates and considered decisions.
Climb the ladder only as far as you must. Put the ask first and the time zone in the deadline.
Use UTC to find overlap. And build trust by keeping, or honestly renegotiating, every promise.

Tools, workflow and delivery: from brief to written decision
Tools, workflow and delivery.
This is the video for module two of Remote Work and Team Collaboration.
Why this matters
Remote work goes wrong in the gaps
Files on personal laptops
Decisions buried in private chats
Two people each think the other owns it
Fix: one written source of truth
A distributed team lives inside its tools. When files sit on personal laptops and decisions are buried in private chats, the team spends hours searching and asking.
Work also falls into gaps, like two people each thinking the other owns a task.
The fix is a single source of truth. For each kind of information, the team agrees one place where the current version lives. Chat only points to it.
Your workspace
One home for each kind of work
Files: edit the shared file, no attachments
Tasks: if it is not on the board, not agreed
Messaging: use threads, point to sources
Meetings: agenda before, summary after
Handbook: answer a repeated question once
Think of five layers. Files and documents: edit the shared file, and never email attachments back and forth.
Tasks: if it is not on the task board, it is not agreed work.
Messaging for quick questions, with decisions posted in the document. Meetings with an agenda before and a summary after.
And a small handbook called How we work. Answer a repeated question once, in writing, then link to it.
You do not need every paid tool. Agree which tool does which job, and stop using the others for that job.
Step by step
Tidy a shared drive
One folder per year, then per project
Five fixed subfolders in each project
Name files: date, project, type, version
Share links, not attachments
Put the date first as YYYY-MM-DD so files sort in order.
For example, Halima's programme drive had files named final report, final report 2, and FINAL final. Nobody knew which was current.
She created one top-level folder per year, then one per project.
Inside each project she fixed five subfolders, such as Admin, Plans, Field Data, Reports and Media.
She set a naming pattern: date, project code, document type, version.
Then she asked coordinators to share links, not attachments, on WhatsApp. Now they find the current report in seconds.
Put the date first, year, month, day, so files sort in date order on any device.
Keep it safe
Protect the shared workspace
Turn it on for every work account, including WhatsApp, email and the drive.
Share personal data with named people only. Remove leavers' access the same day.
Fake 'document shared with you' emails steal passwords. Open the drive from your own bookmark.
Shared drives hold personal data, so protect them. Turn on two-step verification for every work account.
Give the least access needed. Do not share files with personal data with anyone with the link. When someone leaves, remove their access the same day.
And watch for fake document shared with you emails. If unsure, open the drive from your own bookmark, not the email link.
Driver: gets the decision made on time
Approver: the one person who decides
Contributors: a voice, not a vote
Informed: told once it is decided
Every task needs one named owner. For decisions, the DACI framework gives four roles.
The Driver gathers information and gets the decision made by the agreed date. The Approver is the one person who decides.
Contributors give expert input, a voice but not a vote. The Informed are told once it is decided.
Naming these roles ends decisions that are discussed for weeks and never made.
Worked example
Kemi's flyer decision
For example, Kemi owns a health awareness campaign with a team in Lagos, Port Harcourt and Accra.
5,000 flyers, about 45 each
3,000 flyers, about 55 each
Naira prices are approximate quotes.
Every Friday Kemi posts a status update in the same five parts: status, done, next, blocked, and decisions needed.
This week her status is At risk, because the flyer artwork is 3 days late.
Her decision needed: print 5,000 flyers at about 45 naira each, about 225,000 naira, or 3,000 at about 55 naira each, about 165,000 naira.
She names the Driver, herself, and the Approver, Bola. She recommends 3,000, because 38 volunteers can hand out about 80 each.
Bola approves in a comment, and Kemi logs the decision with the date and the reason.
Meetings that earn their time
Ask first: could this be a document?
Agenda 24 hours before, with pre-reads
Name roles: facilitator, note-taker
Read back actions with owners and dates
Post the summary within one working day
The meeting is not finished until the summary is posted.
A one-hour call with eight people uses eight hours of team time, plus data costs. So first ask: could this be a document with comments?
If you meet, post the agenda at least 24 hours before. Write each item as a question with the outcome you need.
Name a facilitator and a note-taker, and rotate them so the same person is not always taking notes.
End with the actions read aloud, with owners and dates. Then post a short summary within one working day.
People who could not attend must be able to act on it. Copy each decision into the decision log.
Key points
Remember
One home for each kind of information
Date-first file names, links not attachments
One owner per task; one Approver per decision
Weekly update: status, done, next, blocked, decide
Agenda before, written summary after
To remember. Give each kind of information one home, and name files date first.
Give every task one owner and every decision one Approver.
Post a weekly update in a fixed format. Mark work At risk the moment you doubt the date. And make every meeting end with a written summary.

Diagnose, price and lead: improving a distributed team
Diagnose, price and lead: improving a distributed team.
This is the video for module three of Remote Work and Team Collaboration.
Why this matters
Find how the team really works
Teams describe how they wish they worked
Ask for evidence: show me
Talk across levels and locations
Report patterns, not names
Whether you join a remote team, lead it, or advise it, your first job is to understand how work really flows. Teams often describe the way they wish they worked.
So ask for evidence, not just opinions. Where is the current budget? Show me.
Talk to people at different levels and locations, including someone who joined recently. Keep what they say confidential, and report patterns, not names.
The audit
Score eight areas from 1 to 5
1: no shared practice
3: a practice, used unevenly
5: written, and most people follow it
Add the scores; find the lowest areas
Scores start a conversation. Show the evidence for each one.
Score eight areas, such as channels, source of truth, ownership, meetings and decisions. A score of 1 means no shared practice.
3 means a practice exists but is used unevenly. 5 means a written practice that most people follow.
For example, Grace reviewed a volunteer network and scored 17 out of 40. It took 11 minutes and three people to find the current volunteer list, and two versions disagreed by 23 names.
Scores are a tool for conversation, not a verdict. So show the evidence behind every number.
What to fix first
Impact and effort
High impact, low effort. For Grace: a shared decision log and one master volunteer list.
High impact, high effort. For Grace: a full handbook, next quarter.
Low value and costly. For Grace: buying a paid tool, because the problem is habit.
Do not try to fix everything. Place each fix by how much it helps against how hard it is.
Start with quick wins. For Grace, a decision log and one master volunteer list take a few hours each.
Plan the big projects carefully, like a full handbook for the following quarter.
And avoid costly, low-value work. Buying a paid project tool would not help, because the problem is habit, not software.
Worked example
Pricing a 10-day project
For example, Bimpe, a consultant in Ibadan, prices a project for an NGO with 15 staff.
Base: 10 days x 80,000
Contingency, 10%
Illustrative naira figures, not market rates.
Turn each recommendation into a deliverable that can be checked, then price it as a day rate times estimated days.
Bimpe aims for 800,000 naira a month and expects to bill about 10 days, so her day rate is 80,000 naira.
She estimates 10 days of work, which gives a base of 800,000 naira. She adds 10 percent for unknowns, 80,000 naira.
Her fixed price is 880,000 naira. Half is paid on signing, and half when the deliverables are accepted.
She also writes what is out of scope, like buying paid software. These figures are illustrative, not market rates.
Protect the scope
When an extra request arrives
Describe the new request briefly
Estimate extra days and cost
State the effect on the timeline
Ask the approver to accept in writing
Start extra work only after written approval.
Scope creep often arrives as a casual WhatsApp message: while you are at it, can you also set up the board for finance? Do not refuse, and do not silently agree. Send a short change request.
Describe the request, and estimate the cost. For example, 2 extra days times 80,000 is 160,000 naira.
Say how the timeline moves, and ask the named approver to accept in writing. An email reply is enough.
Money safety
Confirm bank details by phone first
Doubt sudden new account messages
Invoice in your registered business name
Get written acceptance by email
Protect the money too. Confirm bank details by phone with a known contact before any transfer.
Be suspicious of sudden new account instructions by email or WhatsApp. It is a common fraud pattern.
If you are registered with the CAC, invoice in that name. And keep the client's written acceptance as your record.
Your own system
Capture every I will within the hour
Monday: choose three key outcomes
Time-block and protect focus work
Post start-of-day and end-of-day lines
Friday: review and renegotiate early
Leaders are trusted when their own work is reliable and visible. Every time you say I will, add it to one list within the hour, with a date.
On Monday choose the three most important outcomes, and block focus time for them.
Post a short start-of-day and end-of-day line. On Friday, check every commitment and renegotiate early.
Uche tracked 14 commitments and found her one late item was promised on a call and never captured. Now she writes it down after every call.
Key points
Remember
Ask for evidence, score eight areas
Quick wins first; state your limits
Price: day rate x days, plus contingency
Change requests in writing before extra work
Capture every promise; renegotiate early
To remember. Diagnose with evidence and score eight areas. Fix quick wins first.
Price from a day rate and estimated days, with a stated contingency and clear payment terms.
Handle extra requests in writing. And keep your own promises visible, renegotiating early instead of missing silently.
